summary: Redefines the wire format of the Type Bit Map field in the DNSSEC NSEC record so it can cover the full space of resource record types. It was replaced by RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035.

plainLanguage.summary: DNSSEC keeps a checklist of which kinds of records exist. This document made the checklist big enough for all kinds. It was replaced by RFCs 4033, 4034 and 4035.

questions: how does nsec list record types
what is nsec type bit map
subtitle: A bigger checklist of which record types exist in DNSSEC.

tldr.problem: The original DNSSEC NSEC record could only list which of the first 127 record types exist at a name. When new types were added, DNSSEC had no way to prove they did not exist.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3845 redefines the Type Bit Map field to split the full 16-bit type space into 256 window blocks, each covering 256 record types. This scales to any future type.
tldr.outcome: DNSSEC can now securely answer 'does this record type exist' for any of the 65,536 possible types, with a simple, efficient encoding.

today: RFC 3845 was superseded by RFCs 4033, 4034, and 4035, which consolidated and updated DNSSEC. The Type Bit Map format defined here remains the standard way to encode record type information in NSEC records.

sections.title: The Problem with Limited Type Space
sections.content:
DNSSEC uses the NSEC record to prove that a name or a record type does not exist at a name (authenticated denial of existence). The NSEC record lists which record types are present at a name; anything not listed is proven not to exist.

Earlier DNSSEC rules (in RFC 2535, replaced by RFC 3755) encoded this list in a Type Bit Map that could only handle the first 127 record types. A bit was reserved for an extension mechanism, but it was never implemented. As DNS grew, new types (like TLSA, CAA, and others) were assigned numbers above 127, and DNSSEC had no way to list whether they existed.

RFC 3845 solves this by redefining the encoding to cover all 65,536 possible type codes.
sections.plainLanguage: DNSSEC needs to prove that certain types of records do not exist. The old way only worked for a small set of types. This RFC made it work for all of them.

sections.title: The New Type Bit Map Format
sections.content:
The Type Bit Map field now splits the 16-bit RR type space into 256 window blocks. Each block represents 256 consecutive type codes. The 16-bit type number is split into two bytes: the high byte is the window number (0 to 255), and the low byte is the bit position within the window.

For each window that contains at least one active type, the NSEC record includes: a window number (1 byte), a bitmap length (1 byte, from 1 to 32), and up to 32 bytes of bitmap (256 bits). Each bit set to 1 means a type exists; each 0 means it does not.

Window blocks are encoded in increasing numerical order, and trailing zero bytes are omitted to save space. This makes the encoding efficient for zones with sparse type coverage.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine 256 mailboxes in a row, each labeled with numbers 0 to 255. Then another 256 rows, each starting from a multiple of 256. A checklist marks which mailboxes have mail. This scales to any number you need.

sections.title: NSEC Record Structure
sections.content:
An NSEC record contains two main fields: the Next Domain Name (the next name in canonical order within the zone) and the List of Type Bit Map(s) (the record types present at this name).

Example NSEC record at alfa.example.com: it names host.example.com as the next name and lists that A, MX, RRSIG, NSEC, and TYPE1234 records exist at alfa.example.com. The type bit map encodes this list using the window blocks defined above, with high efficiency for the common case of a few types per name.
sections.plainLanguage: Each NSEC record says 'the next name is X' and 'at this name, these types exist'. Both pieces are needed to prove negative answers.

sections.title: Encoding Rules and Efficiency
sections.content:
Window blocks are encoded in order, and trailing zero bytes within a block are omitted. This keeps the encoding compact for most names, which have only a few types.

Three special rules ensure correctness:

  • Bit 0 of window block 0 (type 0, which does not exist) MUST be set to 0.
  • Bits for Meta-TYPEs and QTYPEs (special query types defined in RFC 2929) MUST be set to 0, since they do not appear in zone data.
  • Blocks with no types present MUST be omitted entirely.

The result is an NSEC record that can represent any zone with all possible types present in roughly 8.5 kilobytes, while typical zones with few types per name are much smaller.
sections.plainLanguage: The encoding is designed to be as small as possible for normal cases, while still supporting the full universe of types.

sections.title: Wildcard Handling
sections.content: If a zone contains a wildcard name (one starting with '*'), the wildcard label is treated as a literal symbol in the NSEC record. Wildcard expansion does not change how the name appears in the Next Domain Name field. RFC 2535 describes how wildcards interact with authenticated denial of existence.
sections.plainLanguage: Wildcard names in DNS are expanded when looked up, but in NSEC records they are written as-is for clarity.

fields.name: Window Number
fields.desc: Window block number, 0 to 255. Each window covers 256 types.

fields.name: Bitmap Length
fields.desc: Number of octets in the bitmap, 1 to 32.

fields.name: Bitmap
fields.desc: One octet of the bitmap; multiple octets follow if needed.
